evaluationApproach.summary: The AI must evaluate response quality and evidence for the Attacking Coach role, including collective attacking organization, training design, player decision-making, communication and collaboration within the Head Coach's playing model.
evaluationApproach.corePrinciple: Strong responses connect attacking principles to observable behaviors, representative training and evidence-based adjustments, without requiring one particular formation or philosophy.

mandatoryRules.rule: Score the response against the Attacking Coach role, not Head Coach, Forward Coach, generic Assistant Coach or Video Analyst criteria.
For questions requesting a real situation or example, do not award 4/4 unless the response includes the situation, the candidate's action and the outcome.
Distinguish between a generally positive statement and demonstrated competence.
Treat relevant but generic answers as acceptable or good, not automatically strong.
Flag contradictions between the written questionnaire and the video response.
Do not infer expertise, credentials or results that the candidate did not state.
Do not reduce scores because of accent, grammar, speaking speed, appearance, age, gender, ethnicity or disability. Evaluate content only, except when audio is impossible to assess.
Do not reward excessive confidence, length or technical vocabulary unless the content is relevant and accurate.

calibrationOverall.classification: Basic / acceptable understanding, with limited supporting evidence
calibrationOverall.strongestAreas: Head Coach alignment, attacking decision-making, staff collaboration
calibrationOverall.mainWeaknesses: Limited measured outcomes, detailed training progressions and concrete tactical adjustment examples
calibrationOverall.summary: The fictional candidate demonstrates a generally appropriate understanding of the Attacking Coach role, particularly in aligning with the Head Coach, supporting attacking decision-making and collaborating with staff. However, the responses often lack detailed training progressions, verified tactical examples, and measurable evidence of improved attacking behavior. Follow-up should test game-model integration, representative session design and evaluation methods.

questions.text: Can you describe your background and pathway to becoming an Attacking Coach?
questions.evaluates: Relevant coaching preparation and progression into attacking specialization.
strong: Identifies relevant coaching, playing, analysis, education or specialist-development experience.
Explains actual attacking responsibilities, team levels, age groups and progression over time.
Connects prior work to individual attacking actions, unit relationships and collective chance creation.
Shows continuing learning rather than relying only on having played as a forward or attacking midfielder.
questions.acceptable: Describes relevant experience but provides limited detail about responsibilities, environments or development.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Relies only on playing position, goals scored or licenses without explaining specialist coaching practice.

calibration.response: I coached academy teams for four years and began leading the attacking part of our sessions last season.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Relevant experience and progression are described, but the candidate gives no specific development outcome.

questions.text: How do you define the role and responsibilities of an Attacking Coach within a technical staff?
questions.evaluates: Role clarity, contribution and boundaries within the coaching team.
strong: Defines support for attacking principles, player-role development, patterns, transitions, finishing and set-piece contribution as assigned.
Explains observation, planning, delivery, feedback and review responsibilities.
Recognizes that the Head Coach owns the overall model, selection and final tactical decisions.
Works with all players involved in attacking phases, not only forwards, and protects consistent staff messaging.
questions.acceptable: Identifies attacking training and tactical support but leaves workflow or authority boundaries unclear.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Describes only striker finishing, claims control of all attacking decisions or gives instructions that compete with the Head Coach.

calibration.response: I help the head coach improve our attacking organization, create exercises and give feedback to all attacking players.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Understands specialist support and wider player involvement; decision authority and review process are not explained.

questions.text: How do you align your attacking work with the Head Coach's overall tactical vision?
questions.evaluates: Tactical alignment, communication and implementation discipline.
strong: Clarifies the playing model, risk preferences, positional roles, match plan and current attacking priorities.
Translates the vision into observable behaviors by phase, zone, unit and role.
Plans content with the Head Coach and integrates specialist work into whole-team training.
Uses feedback and match evidence to adjust without promoting a competing attacking philosophy.
questions.acceptable: States that work follows the Head Coach's plan but gives limited detail about translation or integration.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Imposes a preferred attacking style regardless of the model or gives players conflicting positional and decision rules.

calibration.response: I ask the head coach about the match plan and build my sessions around those priorities.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Demonstrates alignment, but observable behaviors and coordination with whole-team sessions remain unclear.

questions.text: How do you analyze attacking patterns and opponent defensive structures?
questions.evaluates: Tactical analysis, evidence quality and training relevance.
strong: Reviews build-up, progression, final-third entry, box occupation, transitions, set pieces and key relationships.
Identifies opponent block height, pressing, line behavior, coverage, space and repeated vulnerabilities.
Uses repeated evidence across matches and game states rather than isolated clips.
Converts findings into prioritized attacking problems suited to the team's qualities and match plan.
questions.acceptable: Identifies relevant patterns and defensive weaknesses but gives limited validation, context or prioritization.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses one match or highlight, lists patterns without implications or overloads players with unfiltered information.

calibration.response: I review the opponent's back line and identify spaces we could attack.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Relevant observation, but no evidence of repeated patterns, match context or prioritization.

questions.text: How do you teach decision-making in attacking situations?
questions.evaluates: Perception, option recognition and contextual attacking judgment.
strong: Creates representative situations involving ball, space, teammates, opponents, goal and tactical purpose.
Coaches scanning, timing, risk, positioning, support and the relationship between pass, carry, movement and finish.
Uses questions, guided feedback, repetition and variable problems rather than predetermined solutions only.
Separates decision quality from technical execution and final outcome.
questions.acceptable: Uses realistic attacking practices and relevant choices but gives limited perception, variation or review detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Judges decisions only by goals or assists, prescribes one answer in every situation or removes decision-making through constant instruction.

calibration.response: I use small-sided games with defenders and ask players to decide when to pass, dribble or shoot.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Representative decision-making is evident, but scanning cues and assessment of decision quality are not described.

questions.text: How do you train players to recognize and exploit space in different attacking phases?
questions.evaluates: Perception of space, coordinated movement and phase awareness.
strong: Defines cues such as opponent pressure, line movement, body orientation, cover, ball position and teammate occupation.
Links cues to actions such as support, stretch, pin, rotate, run beyond, receive between lines or attack the box.
Trains space recognition in build-up, progression, final third and transition with representative opposition.
Checks timing and collective coordination, not movement in isolation.
questions.acceptable: Names relevant spaces and movements but gives limited cue recognition, progression or collective timing.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses fixed runs without reading defenders, treats space as static or focuses only on the player receiving the final pass.

calibration.response: We practice runs behind the defense and receiving between the lines depending on the defenders' position.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Shows useful spatial cues, but collective timing and phase-to-phase transfer are not fully explained.

questions.text: How do you structure attacking training sessions to develop individual and collective attacking behaviors?
strong: Starts with a clear attacking objective linked to the team model, match evidence or player need.
Progresses from targeted detail to representative unit and collective situations where appropriate.
Controls space, numbers, direction, scoring conditions, transitions and rest to create the intended problem.
Includes observation criteria, purposeful interventions and a transfer or review activity.
questions.acceptable: Describes a logical practice progression but gives limited constraint, load or transfer rationale.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Lists finishing drills without a tactical objective, isolates technique for the whole session or covers too many unrelated attacking topics.

calibration.response: We start with combinations, move to an opposed practice and finish with a game.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: A reasonable progression, but no clear tactical objective, constraints or review criteria are stated.

questions.text: What attacking principles guide your work - positioning, movement, spacing, finishing and creativity?
questions.evaluates: Coherent attacking framework and contextual freedom.
strong: Defines width, depth, support, occupation, mobility, timing, balance and penetration in observable language.
Connects positioning and movement to ball location, opponent behavior and the team model.
Treats finishing as perception, decision, execution and box behavior rather than repetition alone.
Creates structure that supports creativity instead of scripting every action.
questions.acceptable: Explains several sound principles but gives limited hierarchy, interaction or practical application.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses slogans, relies only on freedom or rigid patterns, or equates attacking quality with possession and shots alone.

calibration.response: I value width, movement, support and letting players be creative.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Appropriate principles, but relationships between positioning, opponent behavior and finishing decisions are generic.

questions.text: How do you adapt your attacking methodology to different age groups and competitive levels?
strong: Adjusts language, field size, numbers, information load, role detail and feedback to age and experience.
Builds ball mastery, perception and simple relationships before demanding complex collective coordination.
Considers maturation, physical differences, training frequency and competition demands.
Maintains common principles while changing method, complexity and expected outcome.
questions.acceptable: Recognizes simpler youth work and greater senior detail but gives limited progression or welfare context.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Treats youth as smaller adults, imposes senior patterns or focuses on results and positional specialization too early.

calibration.response: With younger players I use simpler games, and with older players I introduce more tactical details.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Age adaptation is recognized, but maturation, information load and progression are not specified.

questions.text: How do you integrate attacking principles into the team's overall playing model?
questions.evaluates: Whole-model integration and connection between phases.
strong: Links attacking organization to defensive balance, rest defense, counterpressing and response after loss.
Defines responsibilities in build-up, progression, final third and transition by role and game state.
Coordinates specialist training so it supports rather than competes with team objectives.
Uses common terminology and reviews execution over multiple matches.
questions.acceptable: Links attacking principles to the model but gives limited phase connection or implementation detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Treats attacking as a separate department, ignores balance after loss or contradicts defensive and transition principles.

calibration.response: Our attacking exercises follow the team's game model and we try to stay balanced when losing possession.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Connects attack and defensive balance, but lacks defined roles and measures of execution.

questions.text: How do you communicate attacking concepts clearly to players to ensure understanding and execution?
questions.evaluates: Clarity, shared language and confirmation of learning.
strong: Uses concise terminology, demonstrations, selected video and age-appropriate examples.
Limits messages to priority behaviors and explains the purpose behind them.
Checks understanding through player explanation, rehearsal and observed execution.
Adapts communication by role and language need without reducing creativity or humiliating errors.
questions.acceptable: Explains concepts clearly and demonstrates them but gives limited checking or adaptation.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses excessive jargon, long lectures, public blame or assumes players understand because they remain silent.

calibration.response: I demonstrate the movement, use short video clips and ask players to repeat it in training.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Clear communication tools are identified; the candidate does not describe checking understanding through player explanation.

questions.text: How do you coordinate attacking organization across phases - build-up, final third, transitions and set pieces?
strong: Defines objectives, positioning, relationships and progression options in build-up.
Coordinates final-third occupation, chance creation, box arrival and protection against transition.
Trains reactions on regain, direct and controlled options, and reorganization when the first attack is unavailable.
Integrates attacking set-piece roles, second balls and transition after loss with responsible staff.
questions.acceptable: Covers the main phases but gives limited connection, role detail or progression.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Focuses only on final-third patterns, scripts phases without cues or ignores transitions and balance around set pieces.

calibration.response: We train building from the back, creating chances and counterattacking after regaining possession.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Several phases are named, but coordination, set-piece responsibilities and reactions after losing possession are missing.

questions.text: How do you collaborate with other specialist coaches to ensure tactical balance?
questions.evaluates: Staff integration, shared ownership and consistent messaging.
strong: Uses regular planning to connect attacking, defensive, goalkeeper, set-piece and physical objectives.
Agrees terminology, priorities, session ownership and intervention roles.
Identifies tactical conflict or workload overlap and resolves it privately with the Head Coach.
Shares relevant observations while respecting specialist boundaries and confidentiality.
questions.acceptable: Describes collaboration and aligned planning but leaves ownership or conflict resolution unclear.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Works in isolation, competes for session time or protects attacking metrics at the expense of team balance and player availability.

calibration.response: I speak with the defensive and fitness coaches before training so our plans work together.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Shows staff collaboration; shared intervention roles and resolving conflicting objectives are not explained.

questions.text: Describe a situation where an attacking plan failed. What adjustments did you make?
strong: Provides a specific opponent, plan, expected behavior and observed problem.
Diagnoses structure, spacing, timing, player relationships, execution or opponent adaptation rather than blaming finishing alone.
Explains the adjustment, how it was communicated and its tactical trade-offs.
Reports the outcome and lesson without claiming certainty from a short result.
questions.acceptable: Describes a reasonable attacking adjustment but gives incomplete diagnosis, communication or outcome evidence.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Claims the plan never fails, blames missed chances exclusively or changes shape without explaining the underlying problem.

calibration.response: Against a low block, our crossing was ineffective, so we asked midfielders to make more runs into the box.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: A plausible adjustment is described, but the situation, communication, outcome and trade-offs lack detail.

questions.text: How do you adapt your attacking work to different player profiles?
strong: Profiles movement, speed, receiving, combination, creativity, finishing, perception and physical qualities using evidence.
Preserves core principles while adjusting roles, relationships, starting positions or exercise constraints.
Develops forwards, wingers, attacking midfielders and other contributing players without rigid labeling.
Coordinates physical or medical limitations with responsible staff and avoids unsupported diagnosis.
questions.acceptable: Adapts roles or coaching detail to player strengths but gives limited evidence or collective trade-off analysis.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Forces identical behavior, builds the entire model around one player without balance or permanently labels players by perceived limitations.

calibration.response: Fast wingers get space to run, while technical players combine more in tight areas.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Recognizes differing profiles but risks fixed labels and provides no assessment evidence or collective trade-offs.

questions.text: What indicators do you use to evaluate attacking performance beyond goals scored?
strong: Uses chance quality, entries, box occupation, progression, line breaks, transition threat and set-piece execution.
Includes movement, spacing, support, decision quality, chance involvement and repeated principle execution through video.
Considers opponent structure, game state, possession strategy and sample size.
Avoids treating one metric as definitive or claiming direct causation.
questions.acceptable: Uses several relevant team and individual indicators but gives limited context, validation or connection to principles.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Measures only goals, shots or possession, rewards low-quality volume or ignores off-ball contribution and opponent context.

calibration.response: I look at entries into the box, quality of chances and whether our movement creates space.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Useful indicators beyond goals, but context, sample size and consistent tracking are not established.

questions.text: What has been the toughest professional challenge you have faced as an Attacking Coach, and how did you overcome it?
strong: Explains a specific challenge, constraints and personal responsibility.
Describes analysis, collaboration, decisions and communication.
Provides the outcome, remaining limitations and what was learned.
Shows how the lesson changed later methodology or staff practice.
questions.acceptable: Describes a relevant challenge and reasonable response but lacks outcome, accountability or reflection.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Blames players or colleagues, breaches confidentiality, avoids responsibility or provides no evidence of resolution.

calibration.response: Our team struggled to score for several weeks, so I changed the finishing exercises and talked to the head coach.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Shows initiative, but does not establish the root cause, results or a lasting lesson.

questions.text: How do you measure your effectiveness as an Attacking Coach, and how has your methodology evolved over time?
questions.evaluates: Evaluation discipline, learning and appropriate attribution.
strong: Uses execution of agreed principles, player improvement, training transfer, staff feedback and decision usefulness.
Reviews patterns over time rather than attributing one scoring result directly to coaching.
Recognizes shared responsibility for attacking outcomes across players and staff.
Explains concrete methodological changes based on evidence, feedback or new contexts.
questions.acceptable: Mentions player and team improvement beyond goals but gives limited measurement or evolution detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Claims sole credit for scoring, measures only goals or cannot describe any evidence-based methodological change.

calibration.response: I review our attacking clips and coach feedback, then change exercises when players do not apply the ideas.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Demonstrates review and adaptation, but no longitudinal indicators or specific methodology evolution are given.
